subject: Copywriting
title: War Headlines That Shaped Opinion
description: A 60-second lesson on War Headlines That Shaped Opinion.

hook.text: 'REMEMBER THE MAINE!' filled papers in 1898. That headline helped start the Spanish-American War.

buildup.text: William Randolph Hearst allegedly told an artist: 'You furnish the pictures, I'll furnish the war.'

discovery.text: Yellow journalism proved headlines could manufacture consent. Emotional framing turned public opinion overnight.

twist.text: The Maine explosion was likely an accident. But the headline was already printed and the war already started.

climax.text: From Vietnam to Iraq, war headlines shaped which conflicts the public supported. Words moved armies.

punchline.text: A headline started a war. Words have consequences.

quiz.question: What event did 'Remember the Maine' refer to?
options: An explosion on a US ship

details.summary: War headlines have swayed public opinion throughout history. 'Remember the Maine!' pushed America into the Spanish-American War. 'Dewey Defeats Truman' became a lesson in premature headlines. War reporting shows that how a headline frames conflict can shape national policy and public sentiment.
details.whyItMatters: War headlines demonstrate that framing is power. The same event headlined differently can manufacture consent or galvanize opposition — a sobering lesson about the responsibility of headline writers.
takeaways: War headlines have historically influenced public opinion and policy
'Remember the Maine!' helped push America into war with Spain
Framing choices in headlines shape how people understand conflicts

faq.question: How did 'Remember the Maine!' influence American war policy?
faq.answer: When the USS Maine exploded in Havana harbor in 1898, newspaper headlines blamed Spain without evidence. William Randolph Hearst's papers used the headline to whip up war fever. The phrase became a rallying cry that pushed the nation into the Spanish-American War.

faq.question: Can headlines start wars?
faq.answer: Headlines alone don't start wars, but they shape the public opinion that enables political leaders to declare war. Throughout history, sensational headlines have manufactured consent for military action by framing events in ways that provoke emotional reactions over rational analysis.
